[4] The Appellants' allegations were well summarised by the RPD:

[19] . . . .The Claimants asserted that since 2015 they began following the Baba, "a self-styled 'godman' who has attracted a cult-like following." The Claimants alleged that their problems began in XXXX 2017 when they, their friend XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX along with other Baba supporters, rioted in Panchkula following the Baba's conviction for two counts of rape and criminal intimidation. Following his conviction, and as supported by the documentary evidence submitted by the Claimants, there were violent protests arrests and death at the hands of the local police. A month later, the Punjab police allegedly arrested the Claimant. He remained in police custody for a couple of days. Following his release, the Claimant stated that he returned to the same police station seven or eight times to give statements of the whereabouts of XXXX XXXX The Claimant explained that XXXX was important to the police as he was responsible for mobilizing the followers of the Baba, and the police alleged that he, along with other Baba followers, was planning to kill the judge that convicted the Baba along with other political leaders. On none of these other occasions was the Principal Claimant arrested, and following the interrogation he was left to return home.

[20] The Co-Claimant recounted that on XXXX XXXX,2017, when her husband had already fled to the agent in Delhi, the police raided at their home and she was arrested having not found the Principal Claimant. The Co-Claimant stated that she was interrogated about the location of her husband, which she did not reveal, there was an attempted rape and she stayed the night in the police station before being released the following day with the help of the village council. Shortly thereafter, the Co-Claimant stated that she fled to Delhi with the Minor Claimant. The Co-Claimant and the Principal Claimant have another daughter, who stayed behind in [their home village], and who continues to live with her paternal grandparents in the same home where the Claimants resided prior to their departure to Delhi. Notwithstanding that the Punjabi police know the residence of the Claimant, the Claimants stated during their testimony that the police have not inquired for them at their home since XXXX 2018 although they do ask for their whereabouts with the village Sarpanch.
RPD decision
IFA first prong - RPD correct
Evidence

[5] The Appellants alleged that they hid in Delhi, XXXX XXXX XXXX for six months and the other Appellants a shorter time, before eventually flying to Canada from Amritsar, Punjab. At the end of their BOC narrative, after mentioning their having come to Canada, they added, "Police raided Delhi for us."1

[6] XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that the Delhi police were alerted to the Appellants' address in their city by the Punjab police of his home district, who got it from the Sarpanch who learned of it from their other daughter still at home in their village. The Appellants had no encounter with the Delhi police. XXXX XXXX XXXX explained this was because that their agent was shifting the Appellants from one place to another.2

[7] XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that the Punjab police could find the Appellants in Mumbai or Bangalore because they can learn their location from anywhere, e.g. from people in their home village who would hear it from their family. Asked how merely knowing they were in one of those big cities would let the police find them there, XXXX XXXX XXXX referred to the nationwide interest in the Baba's case. In any event, she added, the police could still arrest them. She did not know, however, how the police would track them down in the proposed IFA cities.3
IFA first prong - RPD reasons

[8] The RPD held that the explanation that fellow villagers could tell the Punjab police where to find the Appellants in Mumbai or Bangalore was mere speculation. As a result, it found the Appellants had not demonstrated that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in either city.4

[9] The RPD found it improbable that the Punjab police would be motivated to engage the IFA-based police to find and harm the Appellants. Its reasons were, first, that there was no evidence the Delhi police took any action after the Punjab police contacted them about the Appellants. The Delhi police had not located them, nor did they have any problems with the police during their six months there. There was no indication, the RPD concluded, that XXXX XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX XXXX have a profile warranting the Punjab police to obtain interstate cooperation.5

[10] Second, the RPD focused on the Appellants having flown out of India, in fact, from an airport back in Punjab whose police were allegedly looking for them, without incident. Based on the National Documentation Package evidence, the RPD found that had the Appellants truly been of interest to the Punjab police, their names would have come up in the airport security systems and they would have been stopped from boarding their flight. The RPD also noted that the Punjab police had not seized either adult appellant's passport, nor was there evidence of any summons or First Information report having been issued.6

argument_evidence.context_text: [25] The evidence makes clear that much of that process is immigration-oriented; it concerns itself with whether a departing passenger has the necessary visa to be admitted to the country of their destination.

[25] The evidence makes clear that much of that process is immigration-oriented; it concerns itself with whether a departing passenger has the necessary visa to be admitted to the country of their destination.
The NDP evidence adds, however, that, as far as security concerns, every incoming and outgoing traveller's personal details are matched against the Black List (BL)/Look Out Circular (LOC) database.
[26] Nevertheless, the NDP evidence shows how few people, even those wanted for criminal offences, are included in that database.

IFA 2nd prong - analysis

[46] A November 2017 article by a University of Sherbrooke researcher18 reports that in India, HIV-positive persons face discrimination. They lose their jobs (as well as spouses, not the case here, and families). This discrimination forces some of them to hide their status out of fear. (The Appellants testified they had told absolutely no one.19) Beyond loss of employment, some HIV-positive persons had been beaten, burnt, lynched, and had their funerals cancelled. The stigma went as far as affecting doctor-patient relations, and some hospitals, both private and public, would refuse to treat HIV-positive patients. REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] I dismiss this appeal.

[2] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX, one of their children who is a minor, are citizens of India from Punjab state. They claim to fear persecution by the Punjab police because the adult appellants are followers of Baba Rahim Singh, the leader of the Sacha Sauda sect that is viewed as anti-national, because they participated in a riot following Baba's conviction for rapes, and because XXXX XXXX XXXX is a close friend of a local Sacha Sauda activist sought by the police.

[3] The RPD rejected the Appellants' claims for refugee protection because it found they could live safely in Mumbai or Bangalore. It also held the adult appellants' HIV-positive status did not render it unreasonable to expect them to do so. I have dismissed these appeals because I agree with the RPD.
Allegations
[4] The Appellants' allegations were well summarised by the RPD:

[19] . . . .The Claimants asserted that since 2015 they began following the Baba, "a self-styled 'godman' who has attracted a cult-like following." The Claimants alleged that their problems began in XXXX 2017 when they, their friend XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX along with other Baba supporters, rioted in Panchkula following the Baba's conviction for two counts of rape and criminal intimidation. Following his conviction, and as supported by the documentary evidence submitted by the Claimants, there were violent protests arrests and death at the hands of the local police. A month later, the Punjab police allegedly arrested the Claimant. He remained in police custody for a couple of days. Following his release, the Claimant stated that he returned to the same police station seven or eight times to give statements of the whereabouts of XXXX XXXX The Claimant explained that XXXX was important to the police as he was responsible for mobilizing the followers of the Baba, and the police alleged that he, along with other Baba followers, was planning to kill the judge that convicted the Baba along with other political leaders. On none of these other occasions was the Principal Claimant arrested, and following the interrogation he was left to return home.

[20] The Co-Claimant recounted that on XXXX XXXX,2017, when her husband had already fled to the agent in Delhi, the police raided at their home and she was arrested having not found the Principal Claimant. The Co-Claimant stated that she was interrogated about the location of her husband, which she did not reveal, there was an attempted rape and she stayed the night in the police station before being released the following day with the help of the village council. Shortly thereafter, the Co-Claimant stated that she fled to Delhi with the Minor Claimant. The Co-Claimant and the Principal Claimant have another daughter, who stayed behind in [their home village], and who continues to live with her paternal grandparents in the same home where the Claimants resided prior to their departure to Delhi. Notwithstanding that the Punjabi police know the residence of the Claimant, the Claimants stated during their testimony that the police have not inquired for them at their home since XXXX 2018 although they do ask for their whereabouts with the village Sarpanch.
RPD decision
IFA first prong - RPD correct
Evidence

[5] The Appellants alleged that they hid in Delhi, XXXX XXXX XXXX for six months and the other Appellants a shorter time, before eventually flying to Canada from Amritsar, Punjab. At the end of their BOC narrative, after mentioning their having come to Canada, they added, "Police raided Delhi for us."1

[6] XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that the Delhi police were alerted to the Appellants' address in their city by the Punjab police of his home district, who got it from the Sarpanch who learned of it from their other daughter still at home in their village. The Appellants had no encounter with the Delhi police. XXXX XXXX XXXX explained this was because that their agent was shifting the Appellants from one place to another.2

[7] XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that the Punjab police could find the Appellants in Mumbai or Bangalore because they can learn their location from anywhere, e.g. from people in their home village who would hear it from their family. Asked how merely knowing they were in one of those big cities would let the police find them there, XXXX XXXX XXXX referred to the nationwide interest in the Baba's case. In any event, she added, the police could still arrest them. She did not know, however, how the police would track them down in the proposed IFA cities.3
IFA first prong - RPD reasons

[8] The RPD held that the explanation that fellow villagers could tell the Punjab police where to find the Appellants in Mumbai or Bangalore was mere speculation. As a result, it found the Appellants had not demonstrated that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in either city.4

[9] The RPD found it improbable that the Punjab police would be motivated to engage the IFA-based police to find and harm the Appellants. Its reasons were, first, that there was no evidence the Delhi police took any action after the Punjab police contacted them about the Appellants. The Delhi police had not located them, nor did they have any problems with the police during their six months there. There was no indication, the RPD concluded, that XXXX XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX XXXX have a profile warranting the Punjab police to obtain interstate cooperation.5

[10] Second, the RPD focused on the Appellants having flown out of India, in fact, from an airport back in Punjab whose police were allegedly looking for them, without incident. Based on the National Documentation Package evidence, the RPD found that had the Appellants truly been of interest to the Punjab police, their names would have come up in the airport security systems and they would have been stopped from boarding their flight. The RPD also noted that the Punjab police had not seized either adult appellant's passport, nor was there evidence of any summons or First Information report having been issued.6
[11] The RPD also found the NDP evidence showed little interstate police communication except for major cases like smuggling, terrorism and some high-profile organised crime.7

[12] Based on all this, the RPD concluded that police outside Punjab are probably unaware of the Appellants and not interested in pursuing them. It also found the Punjab police are probably not motivated to track the Appellants to the IFAs. There was, the RPD held, no credible evidence that the Punjab police continued to pursue the Appellants after they left that state or engaged any authorities outside Punjab to do so. Finally, the RPD held there was no evidence that the Punjab police likely are motivated to make the effort to pursue the Appellants far away from Punjab.8
IFA first prong - Appellants' position
[13] Counsel submits that the RPD erred because:

[14] Though the adult Appellants, who have only grade 10 education, were unable to express exactly how the police could find them, the methods are well documented in the NDP. That evidence shows constant progress and essentially completion in the implementation of several domestic intelligence and criminal database systems across most of India. One can reasonably expect the Punjab police to make use of them.

[15] Although there is opinion in the NDP to the effect that CCTNS, the criminal database, was not very effective, that is mainly simply because many police officers could consult it only on desktop computers rather than their mobile phones. Nonetheless, the majority of officers confirmed that they had access to the system. As a result, it is difficult to determine in which regions of India a person potentially entered in the CCTNS could be traced by the police. Moreover, despite divided evidence on its effectiveness, the primary goal of the database is sharing police information across states.

[16] Though the adult Appellants may not have been charged or had FIRs registered against them, the NDP evidence also shows that the CCTNS contains many millions of entries other than FIRs and convictions. These include police station daily and general registers. Thus, the Appellants may still very well be in that database.

[17] The Appellants also face a serious possibility that their presence in Mumbai or Bangalore would come to the attention of the Punjab police through the mandatory registration of their tenancy with the police, which includes police verification of their identity and backgrounds. According to the NDP that process seeks to identify, among others, persons trying to escape the police of another state.

[18] As for the Appellants having travelled back to and flown out of Punjab undetected: Though the Indian surveillance net is continually improved, it appears it is not always successful, because of corruption and remaining technological limitations. In addition, wanted claimants who make it to Canada are the ones who were fortunate enough to pass through the cracks of the security web. That web nevertheless remains tight and the RPD never encounters its prisoners.
IFA first prong - analysis

[19] Counsel has presented a well-written argument that the Punjab police have the ability to locate the Appellants, whether through active means of interstate police database search or passively having the Appellants' address in another state come to their attention through tenant verification. Still, I agree with the RPD's conclusion that there is not a serious chance they would do so. I find there is no more than a mere possibility they would be motivated to pursue the Appellants out of Punjab.

[20] First, like the RPD I find it improbable that the Punjab police followed the Appellants to Delhi or had the Delhi police do so. Although the RPD made no general credibility finding, I agree with it that there was no credible evidence that this occurred. XXXX XXXX XXXX testimony was that the local Punjab police put the information they had gathered, i.e. that he had gone to Delhi, in their station control room and that as a result the Delhi police learned this.9 There was no evidence, however, that this was more than his speculation and actually happened. As the RPD noted as well, there was also no evidence that the Delhi police did conduct a raid or even ask for him at any of the locations XXXX XXXX XXXX occupied during his six months there. At best, his evidence on this point seemed to be unsupported conjecture.

[21] Second, given that the police were supposedly interested in XXXX XXXX XXXX friend for an alleged plot to murder important politicians, XXXX XXXX XXXX release from custody, even after a bribe, and the fact that he was never held on any of his subsequent reports to the police station, make it strongly likely that he was never viewed as a major suspect.

[22] Another reason the RPD gave for finding that the police were not interested in the Appellants was that they had been able to leave India from Punjab's Amritsar airport using their genuine passports. The RPD held that there was no evidence to indicate that there was a travel restriction on them or that they were known to authorities at the airport for any reason, despite what the RPD found were the numerous security checks applicable. There was also, the RPD observed, no evidence of any summons, warrant or formal accusation against XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and no evidence of a First Information Report having been issued.
[23] In my opinion, the documentary evidence does not justify a blanket conclusion that a person clearing security at an Indian international airport means that they are of no interest to the police.

[24] The NDP evidence does inform us that all passengers are subjected to a security screening prior to boarding, and that once a traveller enters the airport, they go through an immigration check where their passport is electronically verified and their picture is taken.10

[25] The evidence makes clear that much of that process is immigration-oriented; it concerns itself with whether a departing passenger has the necessary visa to be admitted to the country of their destination. The NDP evidence adds, however, that, as far as security concerns, every incoming and outgoing traveller's personal details are matched against the Black List (BL)/Look Out Circular (LOC) database.11

[26] Nevertheless, the NDP evidence shows how few people, even those wanted for criminal offences, are included in that database. Its evidence explains that a list of Look Out Circulars (LOCs) is what alerts exit control at airports to stop a passenger from departing. The evidence indicates that for a state police force to have a LOC issued against persons under investigation or fugitives, they must approach the Intelligence Bureau of the national Ministry of Home Affairs. Further, the evidence strikingly provides that:
[LOCs] are only issued in a very small proportion of cases, against specific requests by an officer no less in rank than a Deputy Secretary of the Government of India, a Joint Secretary of a State Government, a Superintendent of Police, or a Judicial Magistrate. [LOC] notices are not issued in the case of an overwhelming proportion of individuals charged, and even of proclaimed fugitives/absconders. No laid-down norms govern the issu[ing] of such notices and it is generally "high-profile cases," i.e., cases that catch media attention or that are politically sensitive or that involve high-profile crimes with imminent flight risk, which are notified. Most persons under investigation would not be prevented from departing the country, unless they fall into these narrow categories.12

[27] The Appellants allege, however, that the Punjab police were actively interested in XXXX XXXX XXXX and pursuing him in connection with a supposed plot to murder a judge and politicians. That would clearly have been a high-profile case. Had the police viewed XXXX XXXX XXXX as having anything more than a minor connection to it, namely as one possible source of information of the whereabouts of his friend whom they allegedly suspected of personal involvement in the plot, XXXX XXXX XXXX probably would have fallen into the narrow categories of persons against whom a LOC would be issued. The RPD was thus correct, in my opinion, to conclude that XXXX XXXX XXXX having encountered no problem at the airport was a factor showing that the Punjab police are not so highly interested in him that they would expend the time, effort and resources to have him detained in and returned from there.

[28] For these reasons, I find that the RPD's finding on the first prong of the IFA test was correct.
IFA second prong - RPD correct

[29] The Appellants are Punjabi-speaking Sikhs. They have grade 10 educations. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX rented land.13 He said this did not earn enough to support the family, so he had to supplement it with hard, heavy and low-paying XXXX XXXX jobs that were intermittently available.14 XXXX XXXX XXXX did the XXXX XXXX and did not earn any income.15

[30] XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXare HIV-positive. Before the RPD, their then counsel argued that the alleged unaffordability of HIV medication and discrimination against HIV-positive persons in India was relevant both to a fear of persecution under IRPA section 96 and to the second prong IFA test. The RPD found that the evidence did not establish that the adult Appellants' medical condition met either test. Before the RAD, appeal counsel submitted that the Appellants' HIV-positive status is a major factor in establishing, that it would be unreasonable to expect them to resettle in Mumbai or Bangalore. It is now even more so, he argues, in light of the COVID-19 pandemic.
XXXX XXXX XXXX report

[31] At the RPD, the Appellants filed a XXXX 2020 report by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, an XXXX XXXX XXXX physician at the McGill University Health Centre.16 This recorded the history XXXX XXXX XXXX provided that he had been diagnosed in 2005 and had been on treatment in India consistently until XXXX 2018, just over two months before he left India. He resumed treatment in Montreal in XXXX 2018, at which time his CD4 count was low and his viral load significant. He was started and remained on the medication Genvoya and one other drug. Within a short time and up to the date of the report, his CD4 count was much improved and he had an undetectable viral load.

[32] XXXX XXXX XXXX reported being diagnosed with HIV in 2011 while pregnant. She was immediately started on treatment to prevent mother-to-child transmission. Post-partum, she told XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX she was advised to discontinue HIV therapy. This apparently was due both to what she reported had been a "relatively high" CD4 count and financial constraints.

[33] Unfortunately, this had severe consequences. Shortly after arrival in Canada in XXXX 2018, XXXX XXXX XXXX was hospitalised for a type of pneumonia that is an opportunistic AIDS-defining lung infection that occurs among people living with HIV with severely depressed immune systems. She was appropriately treated and started on Genvoya and a drug for the pneumonia. Since then, her CD4 count had much improved and she had a consistently undetectable viral load.

[34] XXXX XXXX XXXX advised that given the adult Appellants' proven adherence with treatment, their disease is likely to remain under control provided they remain on antiretroviral therapy, and they can be expected to have near-normal life expectancy and be apt to work and contribute fully to Canadian society. XXXX XXXX XXXX is of the opinion, however, that that is unlikely to be the case were the Appellants to return to India. Although the remainder of her report can be viewed as advocacy, she cites the sources of the information on which it is based.

[35] XXXX XXXX XXXX cites evidence that in India, despite a policy adopted XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, making antiretrovirals available to all free of charge, only 50% of men and 63% of women living with HIV were receiving treatment in 2017 and only 73% of all people living with HIV had suppressed viral loads. Further, she opines, even if XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXX were to access antiretrovirals, they are not assured a continued supply or one adapted to their needs because drug shortages are a major problem in India. Although XXXX XXXX XXXX notes that there had been a 56% decrease in AIDS-related deaths in India since 2010, she states that the fact that in 2017 four of every five persons newly diagnosed with HIV died from AIDS-related causes confirms that access to antiretrovirals is inconsistent in India. XXXX XXXX XXXX notes that in stark contrast deaths due to AIDS are now exceedingly rare in Canada.

[36] XXXX XXXX XXXX believes that even though antiretrovirals are now free there, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX would probably face significant financial barriers to HIV care in India. That is because, according to a 2007 Indian medical journal report, lab tests and hospitalisation are usually paid out of pocket.

[37] XXXX XXXX XXXX adds that first-line antiretrovirals for HIV such as Genvoya are not available in India; instead a combination tablet is currently first line despite known side effects of anemia and hepatotoxicity. In addition, viral load monitoring for treatment adherence and success is not routinely available there, despite being the current gold standard recommended by the WHO. While CD4 counts are an alternative, they are not as sensitive and are more subject to errors.
[38] Finally, XXXX XXXX XXXX cites an October 2018 Lancet HIV journal report that HIV-related stigma is a major barrier to the achievement of the UNAIDS 90-90-90 goals in India.

[39] XXXX XXXX XXXX concludes her report saying:
While they have demonstrated adherence in the presence of a multidisciplinary care team assisting with adherence support, their immune systems remain precarious. In the absence of such adherence support as would be the case in India, I worry that their health would be in grave danger, and in the absence of antiretroviral therapy, I would expect them to die within a couple of years.
RPD evidence and analysis - HIV
[40] The RPD summarised and analysed the HIV evidence as follows, initially in the context of persecution:

[9] While not raised directly by the Claimants either in their BOCs or during their testimony, counsel alleged that anti-HIV medication in India is unaffordable and that HIV-positive persons are discriminated to such a point that it amounts to persecution.

[10] The Claimants have disclosed two documents regarding HIV-AIDS, the first relating specifically to the situation in India and the second speaking more generally to the stigmatization and discrimination surrounding a diagnosis. The first document from November 2017 states that India has approximately 2.1 million people infected with HIV/AIDS, of which 1.4 million, like the Principal Claimant and Co-Claimant, are aware of their status. The article further states that even when diagnosed, frequently they are not followed by the medical system. In addition, those with the virus are often discriminated against by losing their employment, their partner or their family. The article explains that the stigma has resulted in some individuals being denied treatment. India's HIV epidemic has slowed down, with a 46% decline in new infections since 2010 and a 22% decline in AIDS-related deaths.

[11] During his testimony, the Principal Claimant stated that he was diagnosed with HIV in 2005. Since that time, he has been regularly followed by a doctor and he has been consistently on antiretroviral medication. The Co-Claimant, while being diagnosed with HIV in 20l1, was not on any anti-retroviral medication in India. When asked by the Panel as to the reasons why she was not receiving any medicine for her disease, she stated that her cell count had not dropped to a critical level necessitating any medication. The Co-Claimant stated that approximately every six months she would have a check-up by a doctor to monitor her cell count levels. Neither did the Principal Claimant nor the Co-Claimant state during their oral testimonies that they had been discriminated against or persecuted in India due to their HIV-positive status.

[12] One of the articles cited in the first document provided by the Claimants outlined that in 2017, a new bill entitled the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Bill was passed by the Indian Parliament, the first state in south Asia to pass legislation prohibiting discrimination against those with HIV with respect to jobs, housing, education and hospitals. It also bans staff in public places such as restaurants and shops from refusing entry to anyone with HIV or AIDS. In addition, in April 2017, there was a change in policy in India which ensured that all people living with HIV in India had access to antiretrovirals free of charge.

[13] With respect to this change of policy, the XXXX Letter makes reference to an article by UNAIDS, where Steve Kraus, the Director of the UNAIDS Regional Support Team for Asia and the Pacific stated that, "[t]he Government of India is showing bold leadership and commitment to people living with HIV (...) [t]his new policy will bring life-saving treatment within reach of more than one million people living with HIV. It will keep individuals, families and communities healthy and productive and ensure that India ends its AIDS epidemic by 2030.

[14] After considering all the evidence, the Panel finds that the Claimants have not established that they would, on a balance of probabilities, face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk, within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, should they return to India on the basis of their HIV-positive status.

[41] Analysing the HIV evidence for the IFA second prong test, the RPD held:
While the Panel recognizes that there might be misconceptions about HIV/AIDS as well as discrimination in India, the Panel finds, based on testimony and the objective documentary evidence previously described, that the Claimants have not to date and would not, should they return to India, be barred from accessing healthcare facilities, medication, jobs or schooling for the Minor Claimant. As of late, positive steps have been made by the Indian government to combat discrimination by those suffering from an HIV positive diagnosis.17
IFA 2nd prong - Appellants' position
[42] Counsel submits that:

[43] The RPD's errors concern the level of access to medical care for HIV-positive persons and discrimination they face. While the government efforts the RPD cited may be laudable, they should not be considered without results. The documentary evidence filed shows the discrimination is still serious in India. It can affect employment, medical care and also the minor claimant's access to education even if she does not have the virus.

[44] What is more, the new evidence explains that the COVID-19 situation in India, the country third most affected by the pandemic, makes access to the retroviral medications necessary for the Appellants' survival difficult. In fact, it is NGOs who circulate to try to deliver these to homes in dangerous conditions.

[45] Thus, the Appellants' access to their vital medications would be uncertain, especially considering that they would return to India after several years' absence and would be uprooted in the IFAs from their home regions.
IFA 2nd prong - analysis

[46] A November 2017 article by a University of Sherbrooke researcher18 reports that in India, HIV-positive persons face discrimination. They lose their jobs (as well as spouses, not the case here, and families). This discrimination forces some of them to hide their status out of fear. (The Appellants testified they had told absolutely no one.19) Beyond loss of employment, some HIV-positive persons had been beaten, burnt, lynched, and had their funerals cancelled. The stigma went as far as affecting doctor-patient relations, and some hospitals, both private and public, would refuse to treat HIV-positive patients. Although the report notes the April 2017 anti-discrimination law the RPD cited, it mentions heavy criticism by militants and first line persons working to stem propagation of the virus. They say the law could be useful if correctly applied, but up to that [early] time felt nothing really indicated the government would do so.

[47] The article newly in evidence was published July 8, 2020, by The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, a multilateral organisation.20 It describes the work of valiant NGO outreach workers to distribute antiretrovirals to the homes of persons living with HIV in Mumbai, particularly its slums, during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was published after the RPD signed its decision, and thus meets the statutory requirements for admission as new evidence. It is credible and pertinent. I therefore admit it into evidence.

[48] The article advises that COVID-19 threatens to be a catastrophe for persons living with HIV in India. Lockdowns and other restrictions are severely disrupting prevention programs (not relevant here), but access to antiretroviral therapy has also become more difficult. This has made the work of thousands of health outreach workers very important. "We are on a war footing," the director of India HIV/AIDS Alliance, which runs a care and support program, explained, stressing they needed to make sure people living with HIV across India are not forgotten during the pandemic.

[49] The article describes how outreach workers collect antiretrovirals and deliver them to homes, provide HIV care and services and educate persons living with HIV about COVID-19 and how to prevent it. Often this is done in crowded districts where social distancing is all but impossible. NGOs provide home delivery of 2-3 months' supply of antiretrovirals for persons unable to reach the nearest HIV therapy centre. As most of the outreach workers are themselves HIV-positive and from the neighbourhoods of those they serve, they are ideally positioned to make sure nobody is left behind, the report states.

[50] The article concludes: "India is home to an estimated 2.35 million people living with HIV. Since 2010, new HIV infections have decreased by 46 percent and AIDS-related deaths have decreased by 22 percent. Outreach workers like [those described] are making sure that progress continues despite COVID-19."

[51] The documentary evidence indicates that some 40% of Mumbai's neighbourhoods are slums. Given that XXXX XXXX XXXX work experience consists of XXXX rented land, which he could not do in Mumbai (or Bangalore), as well as intermittent hard, heavy low-paid XXXX XXXX, that XXXX XXXX XXXX has no paid employment experience, and that they have 9 and 8 years schooling respectively, there is a serious chance that the Appellants would end up living in such a neighbourhood. Given how many other people survive there in such conditions, that in itself would not suffice to render Mumbai unreasonable or unduly harsh as an IFA.

[52] Does it, together with the adult Appellants' HIV situation and the COVID-19 pandemic, reach that high threshold? XXXX XXXX XXXX cites reported shortages and inconsistency in supply of retrovirals in India. She also notes that, while antiretrovirals are now free, lab tests and hospitalization were, at least as of 2007, paid out of pocket. She adds that first-line antiretrovirals, like the ones the adult Appellants are prescribed in Canada, are not available in India and that second-best tablets with side effects are used there, and that gold standard testing of viral load is not present in India.

[53] The Global Fund is a major multilateral organisation that has received half a billion US dollars in funding. It appears highly knowledgeable about and involved with HIV treatment in India. Its July 2020 report does not indicate that the type or quantity of medication available in Mumbai, including to slum dwellers, is inadequate, or that the treatment or testing available at HIV therapy centres there is ineffective. It states that continued distribution of antiretrovirals by outreach workers will ensure that India's recent progress in dealing with HIV continues during the COVID pandemic.

[54] XXXX XXXX XXXX has great expertise in HIV and its treatment. Nevertheless, given the sophistication of The Global Fund, its on-the-ground involvement in Mumbai and elsewhere in India, and the recent nature of its information, I prefer its evidence, which indicates a more positive picture of the situation facing HIV-positive persons like the adult Appellants.

[55] In addition, I agree with the RPD, and Counsel did not contest on appeal, that despite limited education and employment experience, the adult Appellants have demonstrated ability, adaptability and resilience sufficient to survive economically in Mumbai or Bangalore.21

[56] As a result, I find that the evidence, taken as a whole, does not establish that conditions for the Appellants in Mumbai or Bangalore would reach the high threshold required to conclude they would be unreasonable or unduly harsh within the second prong of the IFA test. I thus find that the RPD did not err in so concluding.
[57] The above is determinative of my decision in these appeals. What follows are additional observations. My decision would be the same without them.

[58] XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that that in Punjab, the Appellants' home state, they don't care about people like him and XXXX XXXX XXXX because there were huge lines one must wait in to get the antiretrovirals. As a result, sometimes they had to return home empty-handed. By contrast, XXXX XXXX XXXX added, in Canada they give her and XXXX XXXX XXXX proper care, because medical personnel respect them, speak to them politely, and don't make them feel stigmatised.22

[59] To my mind, this raises the question: For the IFA second prong test, does it matter how bad pertinent living conditions are in the proposed IFA if the evidence does not establish that they are any better in the claimant's home region? While "unreasonable" and "unduly harsh" are the standards clearly stipulated by our courts and those of several other countries, these still should be interpreted in a way that avoids excessive subjectivity and keeps in the forefront the purposes of the Refugee Convention: protection from persecution. In that light, I suggest, as I understand as have some leading refugee law scholars23, the second prong IFA test should be applied as follows: Is there a serious chance that the living conditions in the proposed IFA would force the claimant to leave the IFA and return home to a serious chance of persecution?

[60] As set out above, the Appellants did not describe the availability and quality of HIV medication or treatment back in Punjab as any better than they appear to be in Mumbai or Bangalore. In addition, XXXX XXXX XXXX analysis of deficiencies in HIV medication and treatment were directed at India as a whole rather than any particular cities or states.

[61] In that light, I find that there is not a serious chance that the living conditions the Appellants would face in Mumbai or Bangalore, particularly deficiencies in HIV medication or treatment there, would force them to leave Mumbai or Bangalore and return to face persecution in Punjab. That is a second, separate reason why, in my opinion, the RPD's decision in these appeals was correct.
DECISION

[62] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
